title: Notes you will actually use
summary_es: Una profesora explica por qué apuntarlo todo no funciona y propone tres pasos para tomar apuntes que sirvan.
prediction_prompt: How do you take notes in a class or a meeting? Do you ever read them again?

segments.speaker: grant
segments.text: Good morning, everyone. Today I want to talk about something you do every day: taking notes.

segments.speaker: grant
segments.text: Most of you write down as much as you can, as fast as you can.

segments.speaker: grant
segments.text: I understand why. It feels productive. But the research suggests it doesn't work very well.

segments.speaker: grant
segments.text: In one well-known study, students were divided into two groups.

segments.speaker: grant
segments.text: The first group typed their notes on laptops. The second wrote by hand.

segments.speaker: grant
segments.text: The laptop group recorded far more words. They almost copied the lecture.

segments.speaker: grant
segments.text: However, when both groups were tested a week later, the handwriters did better.

segments.speaker: grant
segments.text: Not on simple facts, where the results were similar, but on questions about ideas.

segments.speaker: grant
segments.text: Why? Because writing by hand is slow, and that turns out to be an advantage.

segments.speaker: grant
segments.text: You can't write everything, so you're forced to choose what matters.

segments.speaker: grant
segments.text: And choosing means thinking. You process the information instead of just recording it.

segments.speaker: grant
segments.text: So my first piece of advice is this: write less, but in your own words.

segments.speaker: grant
segments.text: Second, leave space. I use only the right-hand side of the page during a lecture.

segments.speaker: grant
segments.text: Afterwards, I use the left-hand side to add questions and key words.

segments.speaker: grant
segments.text: Third, and this is the step most people skip, review your notes within twenty-four hours.

segments.speaker: grant
segments.text: We can forget about half of new information in the first day unless we go back to it.

segments.speaker: grant
segments.text: Reviewing doesn't mean reading your notes again and again.

segments.speaker: grant
segments.text: Cover the page, and try to explain the main ideas aloud, as if you were teaching a friend.

segments.speaker: grant
segments.text: If you get stuck, you've found exactly what you need to study.

segments.speaker: grant
segments.text: I'm not saying you should throw away your laptops.

segments.speaker: grant
segments.text: If you type, close everything else, and stop yourself from copying sentences word for word.

segments.speaker: grant
segments.text: To sum up: choose, leave space, and test yourself the next day.

segments.speaker: grant
segments.text: Try it for two weeks, and then tell me whether your notes have become more useful.

connected_speech.explanation_es: Los dos *as* y *you* son débiles: /əz … əz jə/.
La *t* de *doesn't* no suena delante de *work*.
En americano, *can't* se distingue de *can* por la vocal plena /æ/, no por la *t*.

connected_speech.phrase: you've found exactly what you need to study
I'm not saying you should throw away
connected_speech.ipa: /aɪm ˈnɒt ˈseɪɪŋ jə ʃəd ˈθrəʊ əˈweɪ/
connected_speech.explanation_es: *should* se reduce a /ʃəd/ y *throw away* se enlaza.
